business_problem: University of Arizona researcher Chi-kwan Chan needed faster ways to create stable numerical approximations for black hole simulations because the equations are computationally intractable and new approaches can take years to develop.
solution_summary: At the University of Arizona, computational astrophysicist Chi-kwan Chan uses Codex to accelerate the code and algorithm work behind black hole simulations for the Event Horizon Telescope effort. The scientific workflow starts with telescope observations and the need to model how plasma behaves in extreme environments, but the underlying equations are so complex that even supercomputers struggle and new approximations can take years to invent. Chan uses Codex to generate coordinate transformations, numerical algorithms, and supporting scientific code through an agent skill he wrote, then implements and verifies those outputs before comparing simulation results with observational data. Codex also reviews code and helps catch mistakes in statistics and numerical methods, making the simulation loop both faster and more reliable. In effect, Codex sits between astrophysics questions and software production, letting Chan spend more of his time on research instead of manual coding.
